extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and journalists interested in media studies and the characteristics of tabloid journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the defining features, production practices, legal risks, audience targeting, distribution methods, and manipulation techniques associated with tabloid journalism (print and digital). Useful for analyzing or classifying tabloid-style news output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloid journalism is described as a popular style of largely sensationalist journalism; the size became associated with sensationalism and tabloid journalism replaced earlier labels such as 'yellow journalism' and 'scandal sheets'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories emphasise shocking, lurid, or emotionally charged content to attract readers. Historical context: scandal sheets and yellow journalism specialised in lurid and profane content; sensationalism is a core defining feature to watch for when classifying or producing tabloid-style pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on celebrity news and entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 21st century, tabloid journalism has shifted to online platforms targeting youth consumers with celebrity news and entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content selection often prioritises celebrity gossip, personal lives, and entertainment stories over in-depth reporting. When evaluating, check prominence given to celebrity/entertainment stories vs. public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, simple language and heavy use of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Red top publications (British tabloids) 'publish short stories with simple language and typically use more pictures than other newspapers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabloid prose tends toward brevity, simple vocabulary, and image-led pages/articles. For production, prioritise punchy headlines, short paragraphs, and strong visuals; for evaluation, measure readability and image-to-text ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive sales and distribution tactics (supermarket placement, buybacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supermarket tabloids are named for their prominent placement along supermarket checkout lines; some (e.g., National Enquirer) offered to buy back unsold issues so newer ones could be displayed. Supermarket tabloids are distributed through the magazine distribution channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution strategy (checkout placement, magazine-channel distribution, buyback offers) is part of the business model to maximise impulse purchases. Consider placement and circulation tactics when assessing tabloid reach and commercial priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying for stories and 'catch and kill' practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloids may pay for stories. 'Catch and kill' describes paying someone for exclusive rights to a story and then choosing not to run it (used to bury stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary relationships with sources (payments for exclusives, non-publication agreements) affect editorial independence and the public record. Examples cited include alleged burying of stories about public figures by publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk: libel and defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrities have successfully sued tabloids for libel, demonstrating that tabloid stories can be defamatory (example: Carol Burnett v. National Enquirer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High risk of defamation claims; legal outcomes have at times constrained tabloid recklessness. For producers: ensure verification and legal review where serious allegations are made; for evaluators: note instances of litigation or proven falsehoods as evidence of poor standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandal-sheet practices (gossip, selling positive mentions, suppression fees, blackmail/extortion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandal sheets (precursors to tabloids) specialised in malicious society gossip, selling positive mentions, collecting suppression fees, and in some U.S. cases were short-lived attempts at blackmail or extortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for pay-to-play practices (selling positive coverage, suppression payments) and coercive behaviours (threats, extortion). These practices are historical but inform expectations about unethical tabloid methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format vs. content distinction (tabloid size ≠ tabloid journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all newspapers associated with tabloid journalism are tabloid size, and not all tabloid-size newspapers engage in tabloid journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate physical page size with editorial style. Classification should be based on content, tone, and production practices rather than only format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift to online/digital tabloidization
rubrics_metrics.description: In the early 21st century, much tabloid journalism and news production changed mediums to online formats to keep up with digital media; free daily articles and online outlets have filled gaps left by declining paid newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital format changes distribution, speed, and audience interaction (e.g., social sharing, viral content). Evaluate online tabloid outlets for paywalls vs free access, publication velocity, and use of click-driven headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and misrepresentation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloids 'can often depict inaccurate news and misrepresent individuals and situations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual accuracy, source reliability, and whether stories misrepresent subjects. Repeated inaccuracies or retractions are indicators of low journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience demographics and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloid readers are often youths, and studies show that consumers of tabloids are on average less educated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience profile influences editorial choices (simplified language, entertainment focus). When producing, tailor tone and complexity to the intended readership; when evaluating, consider whether style matches audience needs or intentionally 'dumbs down' content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques used (e.g., cult of personality; dumbing down; framing; media circus; sensationalism; viral phenomena; crowd manipulation; catch and kill; managing the news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists numerous techniques associated with tabloid/media-manipulation such as 'cult of personality', 'dumbing down', 'framing', 'media circus', 'media event', 'narcotizing dysfunction', 'protest paradigm', 'recuperation', 'sensationalism', 'viral phenomena', 'catch and kill', 'crowd manipulation', and 'managing the news'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are production and framing tactics—useful as a checklist when analysing tabloid content. For each story, check for strong personality-centred framing, simplification of complex issues, attention-seeking staging (media events), manipulative framing, engineered virality, manipulation of audience sentiment, and intentional suppression of stories.
